title: U.S. Daylight Saving Time Ends: U.S. Stock Market Regular Session Now Opens at 11:30 PM Eastern Time
text:
U.S. Daylight Saving Time Ends: U.S. Stock Market Regular Session Now Opens at 11:30 PM South Korea Time — BigGo Finance Ask AI Real-time News Market Earnings Call Event Calendar Watchlist Podcast Market Influencers Earnings Call Event Calendar Watchlist Podcast Market Influencers More Ask AI Real-time News Watchlist Holdings Market Earnings Call Event Calendar Podcast Market Influencers U.S. Daylight Saving Time Ends: U.S. Stock Market Regular Session Now Opens at 11:30 PM South Korea Time
 Add preferred source 1 With the U.S. ending daylight saving time on Nov. 1, the U.S. regular session will open at 11:30 p.m. South Korea time and close at 6 a.m. the next day starting Nov. 2. The time difference between South Korea and the U.S. East Coast widens from 13 to 14 hours. Japan, which shares UTC+9, also opens at 11:30 p.m., while Taiwan (UTC+8) starts an hour earlier at 10:30 p.m. Pre-market shifts to 6 p.m.–11:30 p.m. and after-market to 6 a.m.–10 a.m., each pushed back an hour, and South Korean brokerages' U.S. day-market trading moves from 9 a.m. to 10 a.m. Release times for the employment report and Consumer Price Index shift to 10:30 p.m. South Korea time. A bill to make daylight saving time permanent passed the House but has not been voted on in the Senate, so the change proceeded as scheduled. Key Elements 
 U.S. stock market daylight saving time New York Stock Exchange Nasdaq day market pre-market after-market employment report Consumer Price Index Kiwoom Securities Meritz Securities Sunshine Protection Act The U.S. has ended daylight saving time, pushing the opening of the U.S. regular stock session to 11:30 p.m. South Korea time starting Nov. 2, an hour later than before. The close is at 6 a.m. the following day. Local trading hours on the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) and Nasdaq remain 9:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. Eastern Time, but the time difference with South Korea has widened from 13 to 14 hours, changing the timetable South Korean investors experience.
 The U.S. ended daylight saving time at 2 a.m. local time on Nov. 1. The system moves clocks forward an hour during the long-day season to make use of evening natural light, starting on the second Sunday of March and ending on the first Sunday of November each year. This year it began March 8 and ended Nov. 1. As a result, the time difference with the East Coast, including New York and Washington, D.C., widened to 14 hours, and with the West Coast, including Los Angeles and San Francisco, to 17 hours from 16.
 Because South Korea, Japan and Taiwan do not observe daylight saving time, it is always the U.S. that shifts the time difference. As a result, in local time in these markets, the U.S. market opening moves an hour later every November and an hour earlier again the following March. Japan operated daylight saving time from 1948 to 1951 under U.S. military administration and abolished it; it does not observe it today.
 Trading hours before and after the regular session also shift. On Nasdaq, pre-market runs from 6 p.m. to 11:30 p.m. South Korea time and after-market from 6 a.m. to 10 a.m., each pushed back an hour. However, the extended-hours windows South Korean investors can actually use vary by brokerage, so investors should check notices from the firm where they hold an account.
 Category Before (South Korea time) After (South Korea time) 
 Pre-market 5 p.m.–10:30 p.m. 6 p.m.–11:30 p.m. 
 Regular session 10:30 p.m.–5 a.m. 11:30 p.m.–6 a.m. 
 After-market 5 a.m.–9 a.m. 6 a.m.–10 a.m. 
 Day market 9 a.m.–4:50 p.m. 10 a.m.–5:50 p.m. 
 Note: Based on Nasdaq trading hours and South Korean brokerages' day-market trading. Extended-hours availability varies by brokerage. Unless otherwise noted, times are South Korea time.
 Converted to local time for Japanese and Taiwanese investors, the schedule is as follows. Japan uses the same UTC+9 as South Korea, so its opening time matches South Korea's; Taiwan, at UTC+8, opens an hour earlier.
 Category U.S. Eastern Time South Korea/Japan (UTC+9) Taiwan (UTC+8) 
 Pre-market 4 a.m.–9:30 a.m. 6 p.m.–11:30 p.m. 5 p.m.–10:30 p.m. 
 Regular session 9:30 a.m.–4 p.m. 11:30 p.m.–6 a.m. 10:30 p.m.–5 a.m. 
 After-market 4 p.m.–8 p.m. 6 a.m.–10 a.m. 5 a.m.–9 a.m. 
 Employment report/CPI 8:30 a.m. 10:30 p.m. 9:30 p.m. 
 Note: Eastern Time trading hours converted to each region's standard time. South Korea and Japan use UTC+9; Taiwan uses UTC+8.
 U.S. day-market trading offered by South Korean brokerages will also start an hour later, at 10 a.m. instead of 9 a.m. Closing times vary by firm — Kiwoom Securities at 5:45 p.m. and Meritz Securities at 5:50 p.m., for example — so investors should check guidance from their own brokerage.
 Release times for major economic indicators also shift back an hour. The employment report and Consumer Price Index (CPI), released at 8:30 a.m. Eastern Time, will be published at 10:30 p.m. South Korea time instead of 9:30 p.m. According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics schedule, the October employment report is due Nov. 6 and the October CPI on Nov. 10 at those times.
 The U.S. is also pursuing legislation to keep daylight saving time year-round, but it has not taken effect. On July 14, the House passed the Sunshine Protection Act (H.R. 139), which would make daylight saving time permanent, by 308 to 117, but the bill remains stalled in the Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee with no vote scheduled. The change therefore proceeded as planned, and any system change is not yet finalized.
 The timetable change poses a challenge for South Korean investors who have raised their exposure to U.S. stocks: they must rework their trading timing and the hours at which they access information. In particular, with the close now extending past midnight to 6 a.m., the burden of overnight monitoring grows, and the window for responding to volatility right after data releases opens about 30 minutes later. Conversely, with day-market trading pushed to 10 a.m., the overlap with the South Korean stock market in the morning hours shrinks — a development some see as relatively favorable for diversified investors.
 Daylight saving time resumes on the second Sunday of March next year, March 14, 2027. For about four months until then, U.S. stocks and major indicators will operate on the adjusted South Korea time schedule.
